summary:
LunaScope is an interactive 3D planner designed to help determine where and when to land at the Moon’s South Pole. For each Artemis III candidate landing site, it calculates, hour by hour, whether sunlight (power generation) and Earth visibility (direct communication) are available above the actual lunar terrain. It then recommends the best landing site using an explainable decision-making engine. Everything is controlled using a PS2 controller.

Key Features:

- Real NASA data, not simulations: SPICE ephemerides (validated against JPL Horizons with less than 0.0001° of deviation) and laser-measured LOLA terrain data.
- Physics-based predictions, no machine learning: Every value can be traced back to an original NASA data file.
- “What if we land on a different date?” Instantly compare different landing windows. For example, Malapert’s sunlight availability drops from 51.6% in September–October 2027 to 36.4% in March–April 2028.
- Terrain-based shadow calculations: Shadows are computed directly over the 3D lunar surface, including the time remaining until sunset.
- Transparent decision-making: Visible weighting factors and data-driven explanations show exactly why one landing site is recommended over another.
details:
What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

LunaScope is an interactive 3D planning tool designed to evaluate where and when to land at the Moon’s South Pole. For three Artemis III candidate regions (Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, and Haworth), as well as any location selected by the user, it calculates hour by hour whether the Sun and Earth are above the actual local horizon.

The positions of the Sun and Earth are obtained from NASA SPICE ephemerides (DE440 and lunar orientation data). The local horizon is derived from the LOLA digital elevation model (80 m/pixel), tracing 360 directions up to 150 km while accounting for lunar curvature. By combining these datasets, LunaScope calculates the percentage of time with sunlight and Earth visibility, the longest period of darkness, windows when both are simultaneously visible, and the time remaining until the next sunset.

Users can change the landing date (from 1950 to 2149) and instantly compare how conditions change. They can also visualize terrain-based shadows over the 3D surface, along with slope and elevation layers. A decision-making engine evaluates the results according to different mission profiles (solar power, communications, safety, or balanced), recommends a landing site, and generates a printable report containing sources and limitations.

What Benefits Does It Offer?
  • Fast comparison: Compare landing sites and dates in seconds instead of navigating multiple specialized tools.
  • Rapid response to schedule changes: Answer questions such as "If the launch is delayed, will this landing site still be viable?"
  • Clear operational insights: Is there sunlight at landing time? How long until sunset? When is the best communication window?
  • Justifiable decisions: Every recommendation displays the weighting factors and numerical evidence behind it.
Expected Impact

Make NASA's technical data more accessible to mission planners, engineers, educators, and the general public.

The tool demonstrates why the lunar South Pole is such a challenging environment: the Sun never rises more than approximately 6° above the horizon, a distant mountain can leave a landing site in darkness for days, and shifting the landing date by just a few weeks can reduce sunlight availability from 51.6% to 36.4% at the same location.

Tools and Technologies
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SpiceyPy (NASA SPICE), Rasterio and pyproj (LOLA DEM), NumPy, SciPy, Pydantic, and pytest (68 automated tests).
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, CesiumJS (3D lunar globe), Plotly, Tailwind, and Gamepad API.
  • Data Sources: NASA NAIF/JPL SPICE kernels, NASA Goddard LOLA DEM (PGDA), NASA SVS LROC mosaic, and Cesium Moon Terrain.
  • Validation: JPL Horizons, with a maximum deviation of less than 0.0001° across 726 comparisons.
  • Hardware: PS2 controller as the primary interface, with equivalent keyboard and mouse controls.
What Makes It Creative?
  • Combining space, time, and decision-making: Integrates a 3D lunar globe, 60 days of hourly analysis or any selected date, and mission-profile-based rankings into a single tool.
  • Controller-based interaction: Analog triggers control the passage of time, while joysticks allow users to navigate the terrain naturally.
  • Physically accurate shadows: Shadows are not merely visual effects; they are calculated using actual terrain elevation and the Sun's position from SPICE.
  • "What if we land on a different date?" panel: Displays predicted results before applying a new date, using arrows to indicate whether conditions improve or deteriorate.
Key Factors Considered by the Team
  • Scientific rigor: Uses the same reference frame (MOON_ME) for SPICE and LOLA, while accounting for lunar curvature, libration, and the absence of an atmosphere (no atmospheric refraction). All results are validated against JPL.
  • Scientific honesty: All approximations are clearly identified. Seeing Earth does not guarantee a radio connection, and terrain data has an 80 m resolution.
  • Explainability over black-box systems: No machine learning. The physics-based model is deterministic, and every numerical result can be traced back to its original data source.
  • Demo robustness: Precomputed datasets and fallback modes allow the application to operate without an internet connection, API token, or DEM availability.
  • Accessibility: Large typography, plain-language explanations, and support for both controller and keyboard input.
